claim: LLMs can give unsafe or insufficiently escalatory answers to patient-posed medical questions
source_location: npj Digit. Med. 9:241 (2026): Results and Fig. 1, Fig. 3 (p. 3); Table 5 (pp. 4-5); Discussion, 'Specific failure modes' (p. 5)
evidence: Physicians rated 888 chatbot responses to 222 patient questions; problematic responses 21.6-43.2%, unsafe 5-13% across four chatbots. Insufficient escalation is not a rated category: it is documented by qualitative examples (missing emergency precautions for suicidality and miscarriage). Response-level evidence, not agentic trajectories.

claim: Healthcare agents are embedded in clinical information systems and socio-technical workflows
source_location: npj Artif. Intell. 2:31 (2026): Introduction (p. 1); 'Task Processing and Generalizability' (p. 2); Discussion, seventh direction (p. 9)
evidence: Review describing agents that integrate with EHR, PACS and LIS to extract multimodal patient data, in clinical settings with heterogeneous data and time-critical decisions; adoption framed through socio-technical systems theory. The original wording 'tightly coupled socio-technical loops' was not in the source and was rephrased.

claim: Equivalent phrasings yield different triage classifications
evidence: Draelos et al. state that LLMs remain highly sensitive to their prompts and give worse answers with typos or misspellings (citing a survey on misspellings). The previously cited MAST taxonomy (mast2025) has no failure mode for divergent outputs under equivalent phrasings; the closest, FM-2.2 (fail to ask for clarification), is a different mechanism. The defect itself remains constructed.

claim: Specialized agents coordinate commissioning and troubleshooting of drives
source_location: IEEE ETFA 2025: Sec. III-A (Fig. 1), III-B (Fig. 2), III-C (Fig. 3); Sec. IV
evidence: GPT-4o-based multi-agent system with specialized agents for encoder commissioning (setup finder, parameter extraction, template creation, final output, hardware operation via OPC UA) and a directing agent with sub-agents for troubleshooting; human approval before writing to the drive. Evaluation on four commissioning scenarios against expert ground truth and on 341 fault and warning codes against manual entries.

claim: Concept drift degrades learned models, and labels for detecting it are often scarce in industrial settings
source_location: Lobo et al., IEEE CAI 2023: Sec. I-II, Sec. IV and Fig. 1 (pp. 171-172); Tan, IFEEA 2025: Abstract and Sec. I (p. 1033), Table I (p. 1037)
evidence: Lobo et al.: drift makes learned models obsolete and ground truth is often unavailable in industrial streams; on a 1,000-sample synthetic regression stream, prediction-interval width and error rise together after drift (Pearson 0.98). Tan: drift from environmental change, equipment degradation and mode shifts degrades deployed models; continuous labeling is costly; semi-supervised detector evaluated on eight public benchmark streams. Neither study concerns agents or decision support.

Highway agent consumes heterogeneous road and sensor signals
source_location: ComComAp 2025: Sec. III-B and III-C (Figs. 1-2, pp. 292-294); Sec. IV (pp. 294-296)
evidence: Fixed pipeline: an object-detection agent (YOLOv11) and an MLLM scene-description agent on camera images; for accidents, airbag, seatbelt, weather and video-preprocessing agents feed a report-generation agent. Signals include camera images, dashcam footage, vehicle sensors and weather data. Evaluated by manual rating on 10 Cityscapes images and 10 CCD videos. The system does not request intervention.

claim: OOD detection is widely adopted for learning-enabled CPS but does not by itself imply a safety violation; runtime safety monitoring and quantitative runtime verification have been demonstrated in simulation and on a physical testbed
source_location: Lin et al., ICCPS 2025: Sec. 1, Sec. 2 (Fig. 1), Sec. 3, Sec. 7; Brown et al., ICCPS 2025: Sec. 1, Sec. 4, Sec. 5
evidence: Lin et al. describe OOD detection as popular but of limited utility, because OOD inputs need not cause safety violations (cartpole example), and propose STL-based safety monitoring with adaptive conformal prediction, evaluated in two simulated case studies. Brown et al. present perception-based quantitative runtime verification with probstar reachability on a physical F1Tenth testbed. Neither source supports the earlier claim that OOD monitoring is the most mature instrument.
